title: Deployment Strategies
tagline: Blue-green, canary, rolling, and feature flags — how to ship new versions with zero downtime and controlled risk.

sections.content:
Every time you push new code to production, you are making a bet: the new version is better than the old one. That bet can go wrong in a hundred ways — a subtle race condition that only surfaces under real traffic, a memory leak invisible in staging, a database migration that runs slower than expected and takes your entire API down. **Deployment strategies** are the engineering patterns that control exactly *how* a new version replaces the old one, and they exist to manage that risk systematically rather than optimistically.

The naive approach — stop every server, deploy the new code, restart — is called a **big-bang deployment**. It is simple to understand and simple to implement. It is also maximally risky: you have no escape hatch if something goes wrong, your users see downtime during the switchover, and if the new version has a bug, your only option is another big-bang deploy in the other direction. Teams that deploy once a quarter might accept this trade-off. Teams that deploy dozens of times a day cannot.

Modern deployment strategies solve three intertwined problems simultaneously. First, **availability**: users should not see downtime. Second, **rollback speed**: if something goes wrong, how quickly can you get back to a known-good state? Third, **blast radius**: if the new version has a bug, what percentage of users are affected before you detect and respond? Different strategies make different trade-offs on these three axes, and understanding those trade-offs is what lets you choose the right tool for each situation.

This chapter covers the four strategies you will encounter in every serious engineering organization: **blue-green deployment** (parallel environments with atomic switching), **canary deployment** (gradual traffic shifting with automatic promotion and rollback), **rolling deployment** (instance-by-instance replacement, the Kubernetes default), and **feature flags** (decoupling code deployment from feature release entirely). We will also look at how these strategies interact with databases — the hardest part — and how automated observability makes all of them work in practice.

sections.title: Roads, Lanes, and Tollgates
sections.content:
Imagine your current production system as a busy motorway carrying thousands of vehicles per minute. Shipping a new version means you need to route those vehicles onto a better road — but you cannot simply close the motorway and tell everyone to wait while you build.

**Blue-green deployment** is like building an entirely new parallel motorway next to the existing one. While construction is happening, all traffic continues on the old motorway. Engineers drive the new motorway first — testing it, verifying the lane markings, checking the exits. When they are satisfied, a single traffic controller at the junction throws a switch and every new vehicle is directed onto the new motorway. The old motorway is not demolished; it is kept in reserve for weeks. If the new motorway turns out to have a dangerous blind corner, the same controller throws the switch back. No driver ever noticed anything.

**Canary deployment** is like opening a single experimental lane next to the existing motorway. Only a small fraction of vehicles — five in every hundred — are guided into the experimental lane. Traffic engineers watch those vehicles carefully. Are they completing the journey faster? Are there more accidents? After an hour of clean data, they open more lanes: twenty in a hundred, then fifty, then all. If the accident rate spikes in the experimental lane, they close it immediately — only a tiny fraction of drivers were ever exposed to the risk.

**Rolling deployment** is like resurfacing the motorway one section at a time while traffic keeps moving. Section A gets new tarmac; vehicles drive over it while section B is still old. Section B gets resurfaced next. For a few hours, old and new tarmac coexist. No section is ever entirely closed, but rolling back means resurfacing every section again — you cannot quickly un-lay tarmac.

**Feature flags** are the tollgates on the new motorway. A driver might be physically on the new road, but certain exits are gated — a barrier opens only if your vehicle transponder has the right permissions. Engineers can ship the entire new road into existence and then control, per driver, which exits they can use. Closing an exit takes milliseconds; it does not require rebuilding the road.

sections.title: Blue-Green Deployment: Atomic Environment Switching
sections.content:
**Blue-green deployment** maintains two complete, production-equivalent environments called **Blue** (the current live version) and **Green** (the new version being prepared). At any given moment, 100% of traffic flows to Blue, and Green is idle.

The deployment process proceeds in clear stages. First, you deploy the new version to the Green environment while it receives zero traffic — engineers can run smoke tests, integration tests, and manual verification without any user impact. Second, when Green is validated, you update the **load balancer** or **DNS record** to point all traffic to Green. This cutover is atomic: it happens in a single configuration change, and most modern load balancers complete the switch in under a second. Third, Blue is kept running and warm — not immediately decommissioned — so that rollback is equally atomic: flip the load balancer pointer back to Blue.

**Why it works**: The key insight is that the load balancer acts as a single point of truth for which environment is live. Because both environments are always fully provisioned and running, there is no startup latency on the rollback path. You are not waiting for containers to start or health checks to pass — Blue is already warm and ready.

**Where it shines**: Blue-green is ideal for stateless services where traffic switching is clean. If you have stateless HTTP APIs, message consumers, or batch processors with no sticky session requirements, blue-green gives you the fastest possible rollback and the cleanest deployment experience.

**The database challenge**: Blue-green becomes complicated when your deployment includes database schema changes. If Green runs with a new schema and Blue still runs against the old schema, a rollback means running old application code against a new database schema — which can be catastrophic. The standard solution is **expand-contract migrations**: first expand the schema to be backward-compatible with both old and new application code (add columns, do not remove them), deploy and validate the new application, then in a separate subsequent migration contract the schema (remove old columns) after you are confident you will not roll back. This makes database changes a multi-deployment process, not a single deployment.

**Cost**: Running two full production environments continuously is the main drawback. For large microservice architectures this can mean doubling compute costs, which is economically significant at scale. Many teams mitigate this by keeping the inactive environment scaled down or using cloud auto-scaling to spin it up on demand before a deployment.

sections.title: Canary Deployment: Gradual Traffic Shifting with Metrics Gates
sections.content:
The term comes from the historical practice of bringing canary birds into coal mines. Carbon monoxide, which is odorless and deadly to humans, affects canaries first — giving miners warning before the gas reached dangerous concentrations for them. In software, a **canary deployment** routes a small fraction of real production traffic to the new version. Those users absorb the risk first; if they experience elevated errors or degraded latency, you abort before most users are affected.

**How the percentage works**: You start with a small percentage — typically 1% to 5% — and monitor the canary cohort versus the stable version cohort. If key metrics (error rate, p99 latency, business conversion rate) remain within acceptable bounds for a specified observation period (often 10-30 minutes), you promote the canary: increase it to 10%, observe again, then 25%, 50%, 100%. At each step, the new version must pass the gate before you continue.

**User targeting vs. random sampling**: A simple canary routes a random percentage of requests. A more sophisticated canary targets specific users: internal employees first (a practice sometimes called a **dog-food deployment**), then opted-in beta testers, then gradually broader cohorts. This lets you get feedback from users who understand they are testing, before exposing the general population.

**Automatic vs. manual promotion**: Manual canaries require a human to evaluate metrics and decide to promote. Automated canaries use tools like **Argo Rollouts** or **Flagger** (for Kubernetes) or **AWS CodeDeploy** to evaluate metrics automatically against pre-configured thresholds and either promote or rollback without human intervention. Automated promotion is essential when you deploy dozens of times per day — you cannot have a human manually gate every deployment.

**Rollback**: Rolling back a canary is fast: route the canary traffic back to the stable version. In Kubernetes, this is as simple as scaling the canary deployment to zero replicas. No image rebuild, no schema migration — you just stop sending traffic to the new pods.

**Limitations**: Canary deployments require a routing layer capable of percentage-based traffic splitting. Basic Kubernetes Services do not support weighted routing natively — you need a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd), an ingress controller with canary annotations (nginx-ingress, Traefik), or a dedicated progressive delivery tool. This adds infrastructure complexity that is not free to maintain.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    LB["Load Balancer"]
    LB -- "95% traffic" --> S["Stable v1\n19 pods"]
    LB -- "5% traffic" --> C["Canary v2\n1 pod"]
    C --> M["Metrics Gate"]
    M -- "Error rate OK" --> P["Promote: increase %"]
    M -- "Error rate elevated" --> R["Rollback: scale canary to 0"]
sections.caption: Canary routing: the stable version handles the vast majority of traffic while the canary pod absorbs a small fraction. A metrics gate evaluates the canary's health and either promotes it to a higher percentage or rolls it back.

sections.title: Rolling Deployment: Instance-by-Instance Replacement
sections.content:
A **rolling deployment** replaces instances of the old version with instances of the new version one at a time (or in small batches), while the service continues receiving traffic throughout. At no point is the entire fleet taken offline — old and new versions coexist briefly.

**Kubernetes rolling update** is the canonical implementation. Kubernetes orchestrates the replacement using two parameters: `maxSurge` (how many extra pods above the desired replica count can exist during rollout) and `maxUnavailable` (how many pods can be below the desired count during rollout). Setting `maxUnavailable: 0` means Kubernetes must first start a new pod and wait for its readiness probe to pass before it terminates any old pod — guaranteeing capacity never drops below the configured replica count. `maxSurge: 2` allows up to two extra pods to run simultaneously during the transition, speeding up the rollout.

**The readiness probe is critical**: Without a readiness probe, Kubernetes will terminate old pods and start sending traffic to new pods before those pods are ready to handle requests — causing errors. The readiness probe (usually an HTTP health check endpoint) ensures a new pod is only added to the load balancer's backend pool when it has fully initialized, loaded configuration, and is ready to serve.

**Old and new coexist**: During a rolling update, pods running v1 and pods running v2 both receive traffic from the same Kubernetes Service. This means your new version must be backward-compatible with your old version during the overlap window — you cannot change an API response schema in a way that breaks old clients if those clients might receive requests routed to new pods. This is a key constraint that rolling deployments impose on your design.

**Rollback speed — the main limitation**: Unlike blue-green, there is no warm standby. Rolling back means triggering another rolling update with the previous image tag. `kubectl rollout undo` initiates this, but it takes the same amount of time as the original rollout — proportional to the number of replicas and pod startup time. For a service with 100 pods and a 30-second startup time, rolling back takes minutes. During those minutes, the buggy version is still serving some traffic.

**Resource efficiency**: Rolling deployments are the most resource-efficient of the three infrastructure-based strategies. You need only slightly more than your normal capacity (controlled by `maxSurge`), never double. This makes rolling the practical default for the vast majority of services.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# ── Kubernetes Rolling Update Deployment ─────────────────────────
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-service
  namespace: production
spec:
  replicas: 8
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 2        # Allow up to 10 pods total during rollout
      maxUnavailable: 0  # Never drop below 8 healthy pods
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/myorg/api-service:2.4.1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health/ready
              port: 3000
            initialDelaySeconds: 10   # Wait 10s after start before first check
            periodSeconds: 5          # Check every 5 seconds
            failureThreshold: 3       # Fail after 3 consecutive failures
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health/live
              port: 3000
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "200m"
              memory: "256Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "512Mi"
---
# ── Simple Pod-Replica Canary (no service mesh required) ──────────
# Stable deployment: 9 replicas of v1
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-service-stable
spec:
  replicas: 9
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-service   # Same selector as canary deployment below
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api-service
        track: stable
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/myorg/api-service:2.4.0
---
# Canary deployment: 1 replica of v2 = ~10% of traffic
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-service-canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-service   # Same selector — same Service routes to both!
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api-service
        track: canary
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/myorg/api-service:2.5.0-rc1
---
# The Service routes to ALL pods matching app: api-service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: api-service   # Matches both stable and canary pods
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
sections.explanation: The rolling update uses `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 2` — Kubernetes starts two new pods, waits for both readiness probes to pass, then terminates two old pods, then repeats until all eight pods are updated. The pod-replica canary technique exploits how Kubernetes Services do load-balancing: because both Deployments share the same Service selector label (`app: api-service`), the Service balances across all 10 pods — 9 stable + 1 canary = ~10% canary traffic. No service mesh required for this simple ratio. To promote, scale the stable deployment down while scaling canary up, or simply increase canary replicas.

sections.title: Feature Flags: Decoupling Deployment from Release

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The consistent hashing in `_hashUser` is essential: without it, the same user might see the new flow on one request and the old flow on the next (because the random number changes per request). By hashing `flagKey + userId` into a stable bucket number, the same user always falls in the same bucket and always gets the same experience. The `rolloutPercentage` threshold then acts as a gate: bucket 0-9 gets the feature at 10% rollout. This is how all major flag services (LaunchDarkly, Unleash) implement consistent user targeting.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    R["Incoming Request"]
    R --> F{"Flag: new-checkout-flow"}
    F -- "User in allowedUsers OR bucket < 10%" --> N["New checkout code path"]
    F -- "User not in rollout" --> L["Legacy checkout code path"]
    N --> M["Monitor: errors, latency, conversion"]
    M -- "Metrics healthy" --> I["Increase rolloutPercentage"]
    M -- "Metrics degrade" --> K["Kill switch: enabled = false"]
sections.caption: Feature flag evaluation flow: every request is evaluated against the flag rules at runtime. Promotion means increasing rolloutPercentage; rollback means setting enabled to false — no deployment required in either case.

sections.title: Database Migrations: The Hardest Part of Any Deployment
sections.content:
Infrastructure engineers often say the hard part of deployment strategy is not the application code — it is the database. Application containers are stateless and disposable; databases are stateful and persistent. A broken deployment of application code can be rolled back in minutes. A broken database migration that drops a column or corrupts data can take hours to recover from, if it is recoverable at all.

The **expand-contract pattern** (also called parallel-change or branch by abstraction for databases) is the standard solution for making database changes safe across all deployment strategies:

**Step 1 — Expand**: Add new columns, tables, or indexes in a backward-compatible migration. Old application code ignores the new columns (it does not know they exist). New application code writes to both old and new columns during this transition period. Both versions of the code work against the expanded schema simultaneously — this is what makes blue-green and rolling deployments safe during the transition.

**Step 2 — Migrate data**: A background job or migration script fills in the new columns for historical records. This can happen asynchronously with zero impact on traffic.

**Step 3 — Contract**: Once you are confident the new version is stable and no rollback to the old version is planned, run a second migration to remove old columns, old tables, or old indexes. This is the cleanup step and happens days or weeks after the expand step.

**Never break backward compatibility in a single migration**: Adding a `NOT NULL` column without a default value to a large table, renaming a column, or dropping a column that old code still reads — these are the categories of migration that cause production incidents. They are safe in isolation on an empty database and catastrophic on a live production database during a deployment.

**Migration execution time matters**: A migration that takes 30 seconds on a table with 10,000 rows may take 6 hours on the same table with 500 million rows. Large table alterations should use tools like `pt-online-schema-change` (MySQL) or `pg_repack` (PostgreSQL) that perform alterations without taking a full table lock. Planning for migration execution time is part of planning a deployment strategy, not an afterthought.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Step 1: Expand
Add new_email column
(nullable, both versions work)"]
    A --> B["Step 2: Deploy new app
(writes to both columns)"]
    B --> C["Step 3: Backfill
Fill new_email for old rows"]
    C --> D["Step 4: Contract
Drop old email column
(after rollback window closed)"]
sections.caption: The expand-contract pattern makes schema changes safe across blue-green and rolling deployments. Old and new application code coexist against the same database schema during the overlap window.

sections.title: Observability: What Makes Deployment Strategies Actually Work
sections.content:
Any deployment strategy is only as good as your ability to detect problems quickly. A canary that nobody is watching is just a slow bad deployment — the canary users suffer while you wait for the monitoring interval to expire. **Automated observability** is the feedback loop that turns deployment strategies from manual processes into self-driving pipelines.

The metrics you need to watch during any deployment fall into three categories. **Error metrics** are the most direct signal: HTTP 5xx response rate, exception rate, dead-letter queue depth. A new version that introduces a bug should show up as a spike in error rate within the first few requests. **Latency metrics** catch performance regressions: p50, p95, and p99 latency (the 99th percentile latency matters because it affects your slowest users, who are often your most important ones). **Business metrics** are the highest-fidelity signal: conversion rate, order completion rate, sign-up rate. These are harder to alert on because they require more traffic to be statistically significant, but they catch issues that error rates and latency cannot — a new UI that confuses users does not generate 5xx errors, but it does generate abandoned carts.

**SLOs and error budgets** give you a principled way to decide whether a deployment is safe to promote. If your service has a 99.9% availability SLO (at most 43 minutes of downtime per month), you can calculate how much error budget you are burning during a canary and decide whether continuing the rollout is within policy. Progressive delivery tools like Argo Rollouts integrate directly with Prometheus or Datadog to evaluate these metrics automatically at each canary step.

**Structured logs and distributed tracing** help you understand *why* a deployment is failing, not just that it is failing. When your error rate spikes during a canary, a structured log line like `{"level":"error","version":"v2.5.0-rc1","endpoint":"/api/checkout","error":"null pointer in payment processor"}` tells you exactly which endpoint, which version, and which error to look for. Distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry) lets you follow a single failed request across multiple microservices to find which one introduced the regression.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# ── Rollback commands by strategy ───────────────────────────────

# ROLLING ROLLBACK — triggers another rolling update with previous image
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-service
# View rollout history to choose a specific revision
kubectl rollout history deployment/api-service
# Roll back to a specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-service --to-revision=3
# Watch rollout progress in real time
kubectl rollout status deployment/api-service --watch

# CANARY ROLLBACK — scale canary to zero (instant, no redeploy)
kubectl scale deployment api-service-canary --replicas=0
# Verify stable deployment is handling all traffic
kubectl get pods -l app=api-service -o wide

# BLUE-GREEN ROLLBACK — flip load balancer target group (AWS ALB example)
aws elbv2 modify-listener \
  --listener-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:us-east-1:123:listener/app/my-alb/abc \
  --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=<BLUE_TG_ARN>
# Confirm the listener now points to Blue
aws elbv2 describe-listeners \
  --listener-arns arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:us-east-1:123:listener/app/my-alb/abc

# FEATURE FLAG ROLLBACK — no deployment, just an API call or dashboard toggle
curl -X PATCH https://flags.internal/api/flags/new-checkout-flow \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAG_SERVICE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"enabled": false}'
# Response: {"flagKey": "new-checkout-flow", "enabled": false, "updatedAt": "..."}
# All users now see the legacy code path. Zero pods restarted.

# ── Comparison summary ───────────────────────────────────────────
# Strategy     | Rollback speed     | Cost overhead | Complexity
# -------------|--------------------|--------------|-----------
# Blue-Green   | Seconds (LB flip)  | +100% infra  | Medium
# Canary       | Seconds (scale 0)  | +5-10% infra | High
# Rolling      | Minutes (re-roll)  | +15% (surge) | Low
# Feature Flag | Milliseconds (API) | 0 infra      | Dev overhead
sections.explanation: The rollback speed hierarchy directly informs when to use each strategy. Feature flags are fastest because they are a runtime config change with no infrastructure involvement. Blue-green and canary are both fast because the old version is already running. Rolling is slowest because rollback triggers another full rolling update. Notice that `kubectl rollout undo` does NOT instantly restore the old version — it triggers a new rolling update that gradually replaces v2 pods with v1 pods, which takes time proportional to replica count and pod startup time.

sections.content: **Historical context**: The term 'canary deployment' gained widespread use in the late 2000s at Google and Amazon, documented in papers on their continuous deployment practices. Netflix popularized the approach with their **Chaos Engineering** philosophy, where they deliberately inject failures to test resilience — canary deployments were a prerequisite because you needed to be able to contain and roll back failures automatically. The **Strangler Fig pattern** (Martin Fowler, 2004) is a related concept applied to architectural migration: gradually replace parts of a legacy monolith with new microservices by routing traffic to new implementations piece by piece, exactly like a canary at the service boundary level. Feature flags at scale were pioneered by Flickr engineers around 2009 (documented in their 'Flipping Out' blog post) and are now a core practice at every major technology company.

**Common mistakes and interview insights to know cold:**

- **'Blue-green has no downtime'** is only true for the application layer. If your deployment includes a destructive database migration, the migration itself may cause downtime regardless of which deployment strategy you use for the application.
- **Canary without consistent user hashing** causes a terrible user experience: the same user sees the new UI on one page load and the old UI on the next. Always hash on a stable user identifier, not on a random number per request.
- **Rolling with `maxUnavailable > 0`** means capacity can drop below desired replica count during rollout. Under high traffic this causes cascading failures. Default to `maxUnavailable: 0` for production services.
- **Stale feature flags** are the silent killer of codebases. Enforce a flag lifecycle policy: every flag gets a JIRA ticket for cleanup with a target date. Flags left permanently enabled become invisible dead code branches.
- **Interview trap**: 'Which strategy is best?' The correct answer is always 'it depends' — on your rollback speed requirements, infrastructure budget, database complexity, and team operational maturity. Rolling is the practical default; add blue-green for critical zero-downtime paths; add canary for high-risk changes; add feature flags for user-facing risk. Most mature teams use all four in combination.

items: **Blue-green deployment** runs two complete environments simultaneously and switches traffic at the load balancer in seconds — the fastest rollback path, at the cost of roughly double the infrastructure spend. Best for stateless services where clean traffic switching is possible.

**Canary deployment** routes a small percentage of production traffic to the new version, monitors key metrics, and promotes in increments — limiting the blast radius of regressions to a small user cohort before full rollout. Requires a routing layer capable of percentage-based traffic splitting.

**Rolling deployment** replaces instances one at a time with zero downtime; it is resource-efficient and the Kubernetes default, but rollback is slow — it triggers another rolling update rather than switching a pointer. `maxUnavailable: 0` is essential for production services to prevent capacity drops.

**Feature flags** decouple code deployment from feature release — ship code in the 'off' state and activate it via runtime config, enabling dark launches, A/B testing, and millisecond kill-switch rollbacks without any infrastructure changes. The flag lifecycle (creation → activation → cleanup) must be managed as intentionally as the code itself.

**Database migrations** are the hardest part of any deployment. The **expand-contract pattern** makes them safe: first expand the schema to be backward-compatible with both versions, deploy the application, validate, then contract (remove old columns) in a separate migration after the rollback window has closed.

**Automated observability** — error rates, latency percentiles, and business metrics — is what makes deployment strategies work in practice. A canary without monitoring is just a slow bad deployment; automated metrics gates with rollback triggers are what enable continuous delivery at scale.

**No single strategy is universally correct.** Mature engineering teams combine all four: rolling as the default, blue-green for critical zero-downtime paths, canary for high-risk changes, and feature flags for user-facing features where instant kill-switch capability is essential.

quiz.question: In a blue-green deployment, what is the primary mechanism for achieving instant rollback?
options: Running `kubectl rollout undo` to redeploy the previous image across all instances.
Flipping the load balancer or DNS record back to the Blue environment, which has been kept running and warm.
Restoring a database snapshot taken before the deployment began.
Scaling down the Green deployment to zero replicas and rebuilding Blue from source.
quiz.explanation: Blue-green keeps the old (Blue) environment fully provisioned and running throughout the deployment. Rollback is simply redirecting the load balancer pointer back to Blue — no image pull, no pod startup, no health check wait. This is why blue-green rollback takes seconds rather than minutes.

quiz.question: A canary deployment routes 5% of traffic to v2. After 15 minutes, the v2 error rate is 4× higher than v1. What is the correct response?
options: Increase the canary to 25% to gather more statistically significant data before deciding.
Route 100% of traffic immediately back to v1 and investigate the root cause before retrying.
Deploy a hotfix directly to the canary pods while keeping the split at 5%.
Wait 60 minutes for the error rate to stabilize — early spikes are often transient.
quiz.explanation: A 4× error rate spike is a clear regression signal. The correct action is to abort the canary immediately — scale canary pods to zero or reroute all traffic to v1 — to stop user impact. Waiting or expanding the canary percentage would expose more users to a known broken version. Investigate root cause before attempting another rollout.

quiz.question: What does setting `maxUnavailable: 0` in a Kubernetes rolling update guarantee?
options: Zero pods will serve traffic during the rollout — the service is temporarily paused.
No old pods are terminated until a new pod has passed its readiness probe, so capacity never drops below the configured replica count.
The rollout will fail if any cluster node becomes unavailable during the process.
All pods are replaced simultaneously rather than one at a time.
quiz.explanation: `maxUnavailable: 0` means Kubernetes must first start a new pod and wait for its readiness probe to return healthy before it terminates any old pod. This guarantees the number of healthy pods never drops below the configured replica count — achieving zero-downtime rolling updates without any traffic disruption.

quiz.question: Two Kubernetes Deployments share the same Service selector label `app: api-service`. One has 9 replicas running v1, the other has 1 replica running v2. Approximately what percentage of requests reach v2?
options: 50% — Kubernetes Services always split evenly between Deployments.
100% — the latest Deployment always takes priority for new requests.
About 10% — the Service load-balances across all 10 matching pods, so 1 of 10 handles v2.
0% — a Service cannot route to pods from two different Deployments simultaneously.
quiz.explanation: A Kubernetes Service selects pods by label, not by Deployment ownership. With 9 v1 pods and 1 v2 pod all matching `app: api-service`, the Service balances round-robin across all 10 pods, giving v2 approximately 10% of traffic. This is the pod-replica canary technique — simple percentage canaries without needing a service mesh.

quiz.question: Why is rolling deployment rollback significantly slower than blue-green rollback?
options: Rolling rollback requires pulling the previous Docker image from a remote registry, which is bandwidth-constrained.
Rolling rollback triggers a new rolling update that must sequentially replace every pod, proportional to replica count and pod startup time.
Kubernetes does not support rolling rollback natively — a third-party tool is always required.
Rolling rollback requires a full cluster restart, which takes minutes for large clusters.
quiz.explanation: In a rolling deployment there is no warm standby. `kubectl rollout undo` triggers another rolling update that gradually replaces new-version pods with old-version pods — one batch at a time, waiting for readiness probes at each step. For a service with 50 pods and a 20-second startup time, this process takes several minutes. Blue-green rollback is a single load balancer configuration change.

quiz.question: What is a 'dark launch' in the context of feature flags?
options: Deploying code to production servers during off-peak hours (after midnight) to minimize traffic impact.
Deploying new code to production with the feature flag disabled, allowing infrastructure validation against real systems before any user exposure.
Running the new code path in a shadow mode that processes real traffic but discards responses, used for performance profiling.
Hiding a feature from free-tier users and releasing it only to paying customers.
quiz.explanation: A dark launch deploys the new code to production with the feature flag set to disabled (or enabled only for internal users). No external users see the feature, but the code runs on real production infrastructure — real databases, real network topology, real memory constraints. This separates the 'deploy' event (code arrives on servers) from the 'release' event (users can access the feature), allowing infrastructure-level issues to be caught safely.

quiz.question: Which deployment strategy has the highest infrastructure cost overhead?
options: Rolling deployment with maxSurge: 2
Canary deployment with 5% traffic to the new version
Blue-green deployment
Feature flags with 10% rollout percentage
quiz.explanation: Blue-green requires running two complete, identical production environments simultaneously — roughly doubling infrastructure cost. Rolling adds only a small surge (2 extra pods in this example). Canary adds only the canary pods (5% of normal capacity). Feature flags add zero infrastructure overhead — the flag evaluation is a runtime code branch, not a new server.

quiz.question: In the expand-contract database migration pattern, what happens during the 'expand' phase?
options: The old database schema is deleted and replaced with the new schema in a single atomic transaction.
New columns or tables are added in a backward-compatible way so both the old and new application versions can work against the same schema simultaneously.
The database is taken offline and a full backup is created before any changes are applied.
All data is migrated from the old schema to the new schema before the application deployment begins.
quiz.explanation: The expand phase adds schema elements (new columns, new tables, new indexes) in a way that is backward-compatible: old application code ignores the new columns, and new application code writes to both old and new columns. This means both versions can run simultaneously against the same schema — essential for blue-green and rolling deployments. The contract phase (removing old columns) happens in a separate migration after the rollback window has closed.

quiz.question: A team ships a feature flag for a new checkout flow, the feature reaches 100% rollout after two weeks, but the flag code is never cleaned up. What is the primary engineering risk?
options: The flag service will eventually exhaust storage capacity from accumulating flag configurations.
The stale conditional branch becomes dead code — increasing cognitive load, hiding intent from future developers, and creating potential for unexpected interactions with new flags.
Users who cleared their browser cache will see the legacy checkout flow instead of the new one.
The CI/CD pipeline will fail because stale flags are detected by static analysis linters.
quiz.explanation: Stale feature flags are a form of technical debt. The dead `if (!isEnabled(...))` branch will never execute, but it stays in the codebase indefinitely — confusing new engineers who wonder why the flag exists, creating implicit dependencies that interact unexpectedly with future flags, and inflating the cognitive surface area of the code. Best practice is to create a cleanup ticket at flag creation time with a target removal date.

quiz.question: A high-traffic payment API has strict SLOs (99.95% availability). A new version must be deployed with zero acceptable downtime. The team has budget for moderate infrastructure overhead but needs instant rollback capability. Which strategy best fits these constraints?
options: Rolling update with maxUnavailable: 2 — simplest to operate and Kubernetes-native.
Blue-green deployment — atomic traffic switching with instant rollback via load balancer flip, at the cost of running two full environments.
Manual deployment during a scheduled maintenance window announced to users.
Feature flags only — no infrastructure changes needed, rollback is a config toggle.
quiz.explanation: Blue-green is the correct choice here. The requirements are zero downtime (rolling with maxUnavailable > 0 risks brief capacity drops) and instant rollback (rolling rollback requires re-deploying). The payment API is stateless enough for clean traffic switching. Budget allows for the 2× infrastructure cost. Feature flags alone cannot replace a deployment strategy — the new binary must still reach servers. Rolling with maxUnavailable: 0 is a close second but rollback is still slow.
